A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DWC research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, including material relocated between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original MuJoCo policy evaluations, FPGA synthesis results, robustness tests and architectural ablations, including appendix results for DDPG and PPO.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds end-to-end synthesis, quantized-observation evaluations and training-runtime measurements.

M1.justification: Sections 2–3 retain thermometer encoding, trainable LUTs and interconnects, popcount-based action heads and EFD training. Appendix B implements and evaluates the integer-sensor threshold folding and memory-based output decoding already envisaged in v1 Section 3.2; it does not establish a revision to the learned DWC algorithm.

E1.justification: The five MuJoCo-v4 tasks and SAC/DDPG/PPO coverage remain. Appendix B adds evaluations representing 12-bit and 16-bit signed sensor observations, extending input-condition coverage to finite sensor precision without adding a dataset or control domain.

E2.justification: The corresponding return, robustness and ablation comparisons retain the same floating-point and quantized-network baselines. Kresse and Lampert's citation changes from 2025 to 2026 but identifies the same comparison method. The new timing comparison also uses the existing floating-point baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix B adds synthesis protocols that include normalization and output BRAM, plus an FP32-input conversion setting, while retaining the original core-only measurements. Observation quantization is calibrated using ten rollouts and a 1.2 range multiplier. Appendix C adds GPU wall-clock timing across network widths; the original training and return-evaluation budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses investigate whether sensor quantization and previously excluded input/output processing preserve deployment efficiency, and how training overhead scales with network width and observation dimensionality. These address substantive efficiency limitations. The existing noise, width, LUT-input, depth, input-resolution and connectivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 8 newly specifies three training runs and mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting for runtime measurements. Existing return evaluations retain ten trained models and their established uncertainty summaries; v2 does not report an increase in those runs.

E6.justification: Tables 4–5 add quantized-observation returns and fuller hardware resource measurements, including 0.20-microsecond latency for the FP32-input implementations. Figure 8 adds training times, with a reported 7.7-fold Humanoid overhead. These are new measurements under additional settings; Tables 1–3 retain their values. Section 4.3 also corrects the comparator latency description from over 162,000 to over 24,000 cycles.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds mathematical definitions for observation quantization and the folded integer thresholds in Equations 7–8. The related-work discussion corrects the original LUT parameter count from 2^(k^k) to 2^(2^k). No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The main architecture, efficiency and interpretability contributions remain. However, the rewritten abstract omits v1's explicit four-task parity and HalfCheetah capacity qualification, making its competitiveness claim less qualified. The main text still acknowledges that exception.

C2.justification: v2 explains training overhead through interconnect-matrix size, quantifies why the largest model freezes its interconnect, and discusses sensing and actuation limits on useful throughput. It also explains why the FP32-input implementation excludes Ant and Humanoid on the selected FPGA. Existing capacity and connectivity interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a public-code pointer, detailed quantization calibration and threshold-rounding instructions, output-BRAM implementation information, and timing hardware specifications. It also discloses SAC's DWC scale parameter as 0.5 and identifies the EFD defaults. These substantially improve implementation documentation without establishing changes to the original training settings.

R1.justification: The retained related-work discussion gains references on connectivity learning, compact Boolean networks and hardware design, and acknowledges prior logic-gate reinforcement learning through behavioral cloning. Its central positioning around directly learned continuous-control policies remains. Publication and citation-year updates do not constitute new comparison methods.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten around deployment efficiency, wording is polished throughout, and equations receive more consistent numbering. Related Work moves from Appendix A to main Section 6, with corresponding appendix reorganization. The principal method and experimental narrative remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds two hardware tables and a training-runtime figure. Existing figures are relocated or resized, with revised legends, threshold-index labels and width-plot axis limits. These are additions and display refinements within the retained visual style, rather than a wholesale redesign.

improvement.justification: The added end-to-end synthesis, quantified training costs and implementation details strengthen support for the efficiency claims and improve reproducibility. However, new Table 4 contains unexplained 0.00-microsecond latencies and a Walker2d median above its stated 75th percentile, limiting confidence in its exact results. The abstract also loses its explicit HalfCheetah qualification. These issues temper the overall benefit.
